title: Trump–Xi summit: Why the US and China should not underestimate each other
gist: Ahead of the Trump-Xi Washington summit, Chatham House argues both sides are prone to mistaking the other's visible weaknesses (China's property slump and tightening politics; US fiscal dysfunction and polarization) for real strategic decline, when both retain formidable underlying power in trade leverage, technology, military capacity and alliances.

insights.claim: Trump and Xi are meeting in Washington to negotiate an extension of a trade truce set to expire in November, which includes China's pause on rare earth export controls and the US's delay on chip restrictions.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Whether this truce is extended or lapses in November determines near-term risk to rare-earth-dependent supply chains and chip-sector export controls.
insights.locator: A superpower summit is a big deal.

insights.claim: Beijing wants Washington to halt a $14 billion Taiwan arms package as part of the summit negotiations, and continuing US arms sales to Taiwan should be treated as vital rather than as a bargaining chip that could be traded away, contrary to a suggestion Trump has made.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch whether Trump concedes on Taiwan arms sales in exchange for trade concessions, since that would signal a real shift in US Taiwan commitment, not just rhetoric.
insights.quote: Continuing US arms sales are vital, not a bargaining chip that might be traded away for something else
insights.locator: China has also spent decades developing considerable military capabilities

themes.theme: China's underrated industrial and tech power

insights.claim: China holds industrial dominance in electric vehicles, batteries, solar power, drones and telecommunications equipment, and its AI models now match leading American systems at a fraction of the cost and are used by developers worldwide, including many in the US.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Investors should not price in Chinese tech obsolescence; competitive pressure on Western EV, battery, solar and AI incumbents is likely to persist despite China's macro weaknesses.
insights.locator: But Washington should not misjudge Chinese power.

insights.claim: The argument that authoritarian China can only copy and cheaply produce what other countries invent is outdated, since China's AI sector took off only after Xi came to power and has flourished despite his regulatory crackdown on technology firms and entrepreneurs.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reassess any thesis that political tightening will cap Chinese tech competitiveness - the evidence so far runs the other way.
insights.quote: it is time to bin the argument that authoritarian China can only copy and cheaply produce what other countries invent
insights.locator: Many observers will again be tempted to predict

insights.claim: China's innovation model relies on the state picking strategic sectors and flooding them with cheap capital, subsidies and guaranteed demand, while fierce domestic competition, a vast market and the world's deepest manufacturing base move research into mass production faster than elsewhere, though this approach is wasteful and prone to overcapacity.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect continued overcapacity and export dumping in Chinese-dominated sectors such as EVs, solar and batteries, sustaining trade-barrier friction with the US and EU.
insights.locator: China's innovation model is simply different.

insights.claim: China's property sector, once a quarter of the economy, is in its fifth year of slump, and a mountain of hidden local government debt threatens to drag down China's growth for years to come.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This is a structural growth drag that argues against extrapolating China's industrial and tech strength directly into GDP growth forecasts.
insights.locator: Many observers argue that China's economic vulnerabilities

insights.claim: When Trump escalated the trade war, Beijing's threat of rare earth export controls forced Washington into the truce agreed when Trump and Xi met in Busan in October, showing that China's economic weaknesses do not translate into strategic weakness.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rare earth export leverage remains China's most potent trade-war weapon and a recurring risk factor for whether the current truce gets renewed at this summit.
insights.locator: China's economic weaknesses also do not imply strategic weakness.

insights.claim: Beijing has made clear its long-term intent to control Taiwan and economic costs are unlikely to deter that goal, though the military costs imposed by Taiwan's defenses and continued US arms sales have likely already deterred an overt use of force.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Taiwan invasion risk hinges more on military deterrence than on economic sanctions, so Taiwan defense spending and US arms sales are the more relevant risk gauge to track than economic indicators.
insights.locator: China has also spent decades developing considerable military capabilities

insights.claim: The US carries roughly $40 trillion in debt with historically unprecedented deficit spending, now spends more on debt interest than on its military, and rising borrowing costs are jeopardizing the dollar's future as the global reserve currency.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This fiscal trajectory is a structural risk to dollar reserve status and to future defense budgets, relevant for long-duration rate and FX positioning.
insights.locator: Xi will see a weakened superpower

insights.claim: By 2032 US Social Security will be underfunded and Medicare will soon follow, but neither party is willing to cut benefits or raise taxes, so defense, the largest item in the US discretionary budget, may become the target for spending cuts.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch for future defense-budget pressure as entitlement shortfalls bite, a risk factor for defense contractors dependent on sustained Pentagon spending.
insights.locator: By 2032, social security will be underfunded

insights.claim: Trump's approval rating is at the lowest point of his second term, while the Democratic Party is divided over Israel and ill-positioned to lead, leaving the US mired in political polarization that Xi will interpret as evidence of American decline.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Domestic US political dysfunction could tempt Beijing toward more assertive regional moves if it is misread as a genuine opening.
insights.locator: The US ability to address this and other problems

insights.claim: Despite decades of vowing to pivot to Asia, the US instead got drawn into a new Middle East war even under an administration that campaigned on ending such wars, illustrating a persistent US inability to focus strategically on China's rise.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Reinforces skepticism that US strategic bandwidth will match its rhetoric on countering China, relevant to assessing the credibility of US Indo-Pacific commitments.
insights.locator: Indeed, the US has shown itself unable to focus on China's rise.

insights.claim: Despite its fiscal and political dysfunction, the US economy is performing well, the country remains the global leader in emerging technology, its alliances and partnerships are enduring despite recent upheaval, and it retains military superpower status with a foreign policy establishment inclined to intervene if China invades Taiwan.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Counters the 'American decline' narrative; investors should not assume US strategic capacity is degraded just because of visible domestic dysfunction.
insights.locator: But underestimating the US would be foolhardy for China too.
